new_moe_models.analysis: As of April 2026, the leading MoE models for local coding on Apple Silicon and AMD are Qwen3-30B-A3B and its successor Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from Alibaba. Qwen3-30B-A3B has 30.5B total parameters but only ~3.3B active per token, making it extremely efficient. On Apple Silicon with MLX backend and Q4_K_M quantization, it achieves ~87.6 tok/s on M4 Max, ~76.3 tok/s on M3 Ultra, and ~68.5 tok/s on M2 Ultra at 8K context with 128GB unified memory. A 128GB Mac provides full headroom for 128K context windows — even 256K with further optimizations — while a 64GB system is sufficient for 1–32K context. Qwen3-30B-A3B scores 0.80 on AIME-2024 and 0.91 on Arena-Hard, outperforming the dense QwQ-32B at half the compute cost. The newer Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (April 2026, Apache 2.0) raises the bar to 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 83% on LiveCodeBench, still using just ~3B active params per token. On AMD, the MI300/MI325X stack benefits from PyTorch TorchTitan FP8 kernels that deliver near-linear (96%) scaling across 1,024 AMD GPUs, plus a 10x MoE routing speedup via optimized Radix Sort and Group GEMM kernels. For 128GB Apple Silicon systems, Q4_K_M is the recommended sweet spot for memory/speed/quality, while mixed-precision (2/4/8-bit per expert) quantization enables running even 397B-class sparse MoEs with <1% perplexity degradation. The mlx-od-moe project enables on-demand expert loading from NVMe, making 100B+ MoEs like Kimi-K2.5 (375GB) feasible even on systems with less than full model capacity. Compared to Qwen3-30B-A3B, the denser Qwen3.6-27B achieves 77.2% SWE-bench but requires more active compute; the 30B-A3B MoE variant remains the best performance-per-watt choice for local coding on 128GB Apple Silicon hardware.

new_coding_models.analysis: The April 2026 local coding model landscape is led by Qwen3.6-27B (dense, Apache 2.0), which achieves 77.2% SWE-bench Verified and 83% LiveCodeBench, fitting comfortably on 128GB RAM with Q4 quantization. Kimi K2.5 (MIT license, 109B total / 17B active MoE) posts 76.8% SWE-bench and HumanEval in the low-90s; at INT4 it requires roughly 64–128GB RAM depending on context. GLM-5.1 from Zhipu AI leads on SWE-bench Pro with 80%+ and supports 128K context at INT4 on 128GB systems. DeepSeek V4-Flash (MIT, 284B total / 13B active) delivers 75%+ SWE-bench and 91% HumanEval at INT4, though it demands careful hardware setup. MiniMax M2.5 hits ~80% SWE-bench and is among the most RAM-efficient for its benchmark tier. Llama 4 Scout (Meta, 109B/17B active MoE) achieves ~72% SWE-bench and ~88% HumanEval — solid for multilingual work. For 128GB Apple Silicon or RAM-heavy workstations, Q4_K_M (4-bit) quantization is the standard: all models above run within this envelope, with MoE architectures only activating a fraction of weights per token. On HumanEval, most frontier open-weight models now exceed 90% pass@1, making SWE-bench Verified the primary differentiator. The recommended toolchain for local evaluation is Ollama or llama.cpp with GGUF Q4_K_M weights; MLX-format weights are preferred on Apple Silicon for peak throughput. For pure coding-agent performance on a 128GB Mac, Qwen3.6-27B or Kimi K2.5 (Q4) represents the current best local option as of April 2026.

mlx_llama_cpp.analysis: MLX has reached v0.31.1 as of early 2026, with major milestones at 0.21.x (late 2024: mixed-precision kernels, MoE first-class support, Gemma 4 compatibility) and 0.22–0.23 (2025: expanded MoE utilities, memory-pinning improvements, multimodal transformer support). On Apple Silicon, MLX achieves 20–87% higher generation throughput than llama.cpp for models under 14B parameters, exploiting zero-copy unified memory so CPU and GPU share model weights without PCIe transfers. The MLX backend in Ollama delivers ~93% faster decode versus previous defaults. MoE models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma4-26B-A4B, and Llama 4 Scout all run natively in MLX with sparse activation efficiently mapped to unified memory. Supported quantization includes Q4, Q8, and mixed-precision scenarios via `mlx_lm.convert`. For models over 14B, the gap between MLX and llama.cpp narrows due to memory bandwidth saturation on both runtimes. llama.cpp (now hosted at github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) has also made major strides: Metal GPU offload is now default and stable on macOS, Homebrew installation (`brew install llama.cpp`) automatically enables Metal with no manual CMake flags required. Recent builds (b4000+, 2025–2026) deliver 30–70 tok/s for Q4_K_M 8B models on M3/M4 MacBook Pro, with rewritten Metal kernels supporting 32K–128K context windows without throughput decay. KV cache with prefix caching is GPU-backed and robust for RAG and API chatbot use cases. llama.cpp maintains parity with CUDA performance on comparable memory budgets, and for long-context or RAM-edge workloads it outperforms MLX due to more aggressive quantization (1.5–8 bit GGUF) and efficient batching. The two runtimes are complementary: MLX for maximum throughput on macOS with sub-14B or well-funded memory, llama.cpp for flexibility, cross-platform deployment, and edge-of-RAM large models.

coding_agents.analysis: OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) is the dominant enterprise-grade open-source autonomous coding agent as of April 2026, with 70K+ GitHub stars. It runs agents inside Docker sandboxes, integrates with GitHub/GitLab, and natively supports vLLM and Ollama for fully local inference using open-weight models like DeepSeek, Llama 4, and Qwen3.6. With top cloud LLMs (Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5) it achieves 66–77% on SWE-bench Verified, surpassing Devin in independent evals. New 2025–2026 features include a Skills System for domain-specific agent specialization (e.g., vulnerability patching, legacy migration), event-sourced agent memory for replay and fine-tuning, multi-agent delegation with hierarchical sub-agent execution, and Slack/Jira/Linear integrations in OpenHands Cloud. AMD/NVIDIA deployment guides enable local LLM-backed coding agents on Ryzen AI and Radeon workstations. SWE-agent (Princeton/Stanford, 19K+ GitHub stars) remains the research-first scaffold: the new mini-SWE-Agent is a ~100-line Python agent now the default for academic benchmarking, achieving 74%+ patch rate with top LLMs and supporting full multimodal tool APIs. Aider remains the most model-agnostic terminal-based coding assistant, supporting Claude 3+, GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Gemini, and local models via Ollama with a simple config (AIDER_MODEL=ollama/qwen3.6-27b). Its 2025–2026 upgrades include autonomous test-fix loops (run tests → fix failures → commit automatically), full repository mapping for multi-file context, voice/image/web input as context, and tiered model usage mixing local and cloud LLMs for cost/quality optimization. GitHub Copilot has expanded with agent-mode autonomous edits across multi-file repositories. All major frameworks (OpenHands, Aider, SWE-agent) now support YOLO-style fully autonomous runs where the agent iterates without human confirmation until task completion or token budget exhaustion.

data.best_model: Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE, Apache 2.0) — best coding/agent quality per tok/s on Apple Silicon 128GB
data.model_config: Q4_K_M or Q4 4-bit via Apple MLX; 32K–128K context window; ~87 tok/s decode on M4 Max 128GB; fits in ~17–20GB active memory (MoE sparse activation); full 128K ctx usable with 128GB RAM
data.fine_tuning: Fully feasible. Use Apple MLX LoRA (mlx-lm) for Qwen3-30B-A3B or any 7B–30B model. 128GB RAM allows batch sizes of 4–8 for LoRA with 4-bit base. Full-param fine-tuning feasible up to ~13B; LoRA/QLoRA up to 30B+ dense or 70B+ MoE. Expect ~1–3 tokens/sec training throughput on 30B LoRA — slow but functional overnight. PyTorch via Metal (MPS backend) also works for Hugging Face PEFT pipelines. M4 Max thermal management in desktop chassis sustains multi-hour fine-tuning sessions without throttling.
